title: Amazon Product Research Basics: Demand, Competition, Margin
headline: Amazon Product Research Basics: Demand, Competition and Margin
description: A plain-language guide to Amazon product research for beginners: how to judge demand, read the competition, work out your margin and test an idea before you buy stock.
body_html:
Choosing what to sell is the decision that shapes everything else on Amazon. A good listing and careful advertising cannot rescue a product that nobody is searching for, or one where the numbers never leave room for profit. Product research is simply the habit of checking three things before you spend money: is there demand, how strong is the competition, and is there enough margin. This guide explains each one in plain language. It is general information, and no method can guarantee that a product will sell.

1. Demand: are people already buying this?

On Amazon it is usually easier to serve demand that exists than to create it. Look for signs that shoppers are already searching for and buying the type of product you have in mind.

  • Search the main keyword on the marketplace you plan to sell in and look at the first page. Several products with steady sales suggest real demand.
  • Check the Best Sellers Rank on product pages. A better rank within a category generally means more sales, but rank moves daily and means different things in different categories, so compare like with like.
  • Look at more than one seller. If only the top listing sells and the rest are quiet, the demand may belong to one brand rather than to the product type.
  • Think about seasons. Some products sell for a few weeks a year. A product with year-round demand is easier for a beginner to plan.

Research tools give sales estimates, and they are useful for comparing products. Treat them as estimates. Different tools often show different numbers for the same product.

2. Competition: can a new seller get noticed?

Demand alone is not enough. You also need a realistic chance of reaching page one. Study the listings you would be competing with.

  • Review counts. If every listing on page one has a very large number of reviews, a new product will struggle to earn trust. A page where some sellers do well with modest review counts is more open.
  • New sellers. Check whether recently launched listings are getting sales. That is one of the clearest signs that the niche still has room.
  • Big brands and Amazon itself. If well-known brands or Amazon's own products take most of the sales, shoppers may not consider an unknown name.
  • Listing quality. Weak photos, thin descriptions and repeated complaints in reviews are openings. Strong listings everywhere mean you need a clearer reason for shoppers to choose you.

Read the negative reviews of the leading products carefully. They tell you, in customers' own words, what is missing. A product that fixes a common complaint has a real point of difference, and you can explain it honestly in your listing. Our listing optimisation guide shows how to present that clearly.

3. Margin: is there money left at the end?

Many beginners look at the selling price and the factory price and stop there. The costs in between decide whether the product is worth selling. Before you order, write down every cost per unit:

  • Product cost from the supplier, including packaging.
  • Shipping to the Amazon warehouse or to your own, plus customs duty and any import taxes.
  • Amazon's referral fee for the category.
  • Fulfilment fees if you use FBA, and storage fees. Our FBA vs FBM guide explains the two fulfilment options.
  • Advertising. Most new products need paid ads to get their first sales.
  • Returns, damaged units and VAT or sales tax where it applies.

Amazon's fees depend on the marketplace, the category and the size and weight of the product, and they change. Use the current fee schedule and the revenue calculator in Seller Central for your own figures rather than a number from a video or an old article. Then ask a simple question: after all of these costs, is the profit per unit enough to justify the work and the risk? Very cheap products often leave too little room once fees and advertising are paid.

Other checks before you commit

  • Restrictions. Some categories and products need approval, and some need safety documents or certificates. Check the rules for your marketplace first.
  • Intellectual property. Avoid products protected by someone else's patent, design or trade mark.
  • Size and fragility. Small, light and sturdy products are cheaper to ship and store, and they produce fewer returns.
  • Supplier reliability. Ask for samples, compare more than one supplier and confirm the quality yourself before a full order.

Test small, then decide

Research reduces risk. It does not remove it. Once a product passes the three checks, order samples and start with a quantity you can afford to lose. Watch real results for a few weeks: how many shoppers click, how many buy, what the advertising costs and what customers say. Real numbers from your own listing are worth more than any estimate, and they tell you whether to reorder, improve the product or move on.

Common beginner mistakes

  • Choosing a product because you like it, without checking demand.
  • Copying the best seller exactly, with nothing different to offer.
  • Forgetting advertising and returns in the margin calculation.
  • Trusting one tool's sales estimate as if it were a fact.
  • Placing a large first order to get a lower unit price.
